questions.stem: The central problem that gives rise to the study of economics is that
options: human wants are unlimited while the resources for satisfying them are limited
money is not evenly distributed among households
governments spend more than they earn
questions.explanation: Scarcity of resources relative to unlimited wants forces choice, and choice is the core of economics.

questions.stem: Adaeze has ₦5,000 and must choose between a textbook and a pair of sandals, each costing ₦5,000. She buys the textbook. The opportunity cost of her decision is
options: the pair of sandals she gave up
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative forgone, not the money spent or the item chosen.

questions.stem: A list of wants arranged in order of their importance to an individual is called
questions.explanation: A scale of preference ranks wants by urgency so that the most pressing are satisfied first.

questions.stem: A production possibility frontier (PPF) that is bowed outward (concave to the origin) illustrates
options: constant opportunity cost between the two goods
that resources are equally suited to both goods
increasing opportunity cost as more of one good is produced
that the economy has unemployed resources
questions.explanation: Resources are not equally efficient in all uses, so each extra unit of one good costs increasingly more of the other.

questions.stem: A point inside the production possibility curve of a country indicates that
options: the country has reached full employment
some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently
the country is enjoying economic growth
questions.explanation: Points inside the PPF are attainable but wasteful; points on it are efficient and points outside are unattainable.

questions.stem: An outward shift of the entire production possibility frontier of an economy is most likely to result from
options: a fall in the price of one of the goods
a movement of labour from farming to manufacturing
the discovery of new mineral deposits
questions.explanation: Growth in the quantity or quality of resources shifts the whole PPF outward; reallocating existing resources only moves along it.

questions.stem: The question "for whom to produce" in economics is concerned with
options: the types of goods to be produced
how output is distributed among members of society
questions.explanation: "For whom" deals with distribution of goods and services among people.

questions.stem: In economics, rationality implies that consumers
options: spend all their income on necessities
never save any part of their income
aim to obtain maximum satisfaction from their limited income
questions.explanation: A rational consumer allocates limited income to maximise satisfaction.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a FREE good in economics?
options: Pipe-borne water supplied to a home
Textbooks given to pupils by a state government
questions.explanation: A free good is not scarce and has no opportunity cost; goods provided free by government still use scarce resources.

questions.stem: A farmer can use a plot of land either to produce 40 tubers of yam or 20 baskets of tomatoes. If he decides to produce only tomatoes, the opportunity cost of one basket of tomatoes is
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost per basket = 40 tubers ÷ 20 baskets = 2 tubers of yam forgone for each basket.

questions.stem: Production in economics is said to be complete only when
options: the goods reach the final consumer
raw materials have been transformed into finished goods
the goods have been stored in a warehouse
the goods have been packaged by the manufacturer
questions.explanation: Production includes all activities up to the point where goods reach the final consumer.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best defines economics?
options: The study of how money is made and spent by individuals
The study of how society allocates scarce resources among competing uses
The study of business and banking activities
The study of how government raises taxes
questions.explanation: The scarcity-and-choice definition is the widely accepted one.

questions.stem: On a production possibility curve between maize and cassava, moving from a point producing 30 tonnes of maize and 50 tonnes of cassava to one producing 35 tonnes of maize and 42 tonnes of cassava means the opportunity cost of each extra tonne of maize is
questions.explanation: Cassava given up = 50 − 42 = 8 tonnes for 5 extra tonnes of maize, so 8 ÷ 5 = 1.6 tonnes per tonne of maize.

questions.stem: Economic goods are goods that
options: are scarce and command a price
questions.explanation: Economic goods are scarce relative to demand and so have a price or opportunity cost.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a basic economic problem facing every society?
options: What goods and services to produce
How much tax to collect from citizens
How to produce the goods and services
For whom the goods and services are produced
questions.explanation: What, how and for whom are the universal economic questions; tax levels are a policy choice.

questions.stem: Consumption in economics refers to
options: the buying of goods for resale
the saving of income for future use
the production of goods for export
the using up of goods and services to satisfy wants
questions.explanation: Consumption is the act of using goods and services to satisfy human wants.

questions.stem: In a free enterprise (capitalist) economy, the basic economic questions are answered mainly through
questions.explanation: Prices determined by market forces signal what to produce, how and for whom.

questions.stem: A major feature of a centrally planned economy is
options: state ownership of the means of production
profit motive as the main drive
questions.explanation: In a command economy the state owns and directs most productive resources.

questions.stem: An economy in which both the government and private individuals own and control resources is a
questions.explanation: A mixed economy combines private enterprise with public ownership and control.

questions.stem: One major criticism of the capitalist economic system is that it
options: tends to create wide inequality in income and wealth
makes resource allocation slow and bureaucratic
questions.explanation: Market outcomes reward ownership of resources, so income gaps can widen.

questions.stem: Consumer sovereignty is a feature associated mainly with
questions.explanation: In a market economy consumers, through their spending, direct what producers make.

questions.stem: Deregulation of a sector of the economy means
options: reducing government controls so that market forces operate more freely
transferring all public companies to foreign investors
imposing price controls on essential goods
increasing the number of government agencies in the sector
questions.explanation: Deregulation removes or relaxes rules and controls, allowing prices and entry to be set by the market.

questions.stem: The consolidation of banks in an economy, where small banks are required to merge or raise more capital, is mainly intended to
options: reduce the number of bank customers
increase the number of small banks
replace commercial banks with the central bank
build stronger banks able to withstand shocks
questions.explanation: Recapitalisation and consolidation aim to create sound, well-capitalised banks.

questions.stem: A cash-less policy introduced by a central bank is designed mainly to
options: abolish the use of bank accounts
increase the printing of currency notes
reduce the amount of physical cash used in transactions
stop the use of cheques in commerce
questions.explanation: Cash-less policies encourage electronic payments to cut the cost and risks of handling cash.

questions.stem: Under a command economy, a shortage of a commodity is most likely to be dealt with by
options: an automatic rise in its market price
consumers bidding for the available stock
questions.explanation: Prices do not adjust freely in a planned economy, so authorities ration scarce goods.

questions.stem: The profit motive is the main driving force in a
questions.explanation: Private owners in capitalism produce in order to earn profit.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of a planned economy?
options: Consumers have wide freedom of choice
Resources can be directed towards national priorities
Prices quickly adjust to changes in demand
Firms compete vigorously to cut costs
questions.explanation: Central planners can channel resources to chosen sectors, though often at the cost of efficiency.

questions.stem: In a mixed economy, government most commonly participates directly in the production of
options: all consumer goods sold in the market
goods that private firms produce profitably
public utilities and strategic goods that the market may under-provide
questions.explanation: Government steps in where the market fails, e.g. utilities, defence and other public goods.

questions.stem: An economy in which production is mainly for the producer's own use is known as
questions.explanation: Subsistence production is for own consumption rather than for sale.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why a pure free-market economy may fail to provide street lighting?
options: It is too cheap to produce
Consumers do not want street lighting
Non-payers cannot easily be excluded from its benefits
questions.explanation: Street lighting is a public good: non-excludability creates a free-rider problem so private firms cannot charge for it.

questions.explanation: The mean uses every value, so very large or very small values pull it strongly.

questions.topic: Methods and Tools of Economic Analysis
questions.stem: A disadvantage of the mode as a measure of central tendency is that
options: it is affected by extreme values
a set of data may have more than one mode or none at all
it cannot be found for qualitative data
questions.explanation: Data may be bimodal, multimodal or have no repeated value, making the mode ambiguous.

questions.topic: Methods and Tools of Economic Analysis
questions.stem: The phrase "ceteris paribus" in economic analysis means
questions.explanation: Ceteris paribus holds other influences constant so one relationship can be studied.

questions.topic: Methods and Tools of Economic Analysis
questions.stem: Which of the following is a measure of dispersion?
questions.explanation: Dispersion measures (range, variance, standard deviation) show spread; the others are averages.

questions.topic: Methods and Tools of Economic Analysis
questions.stem: A merit of the median over the mean is that the median
options: is not distorted by extreme values
uses every item in the data
can be used in further algebraic work
questions.explanation: Being the middle value, the median ignores the size of extreme items.

questions.stem: Demand in economics refers to
options: the desire of consumers to own a good
the total quantity of a good available in the market
the quantity of a good consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price over a period
the amount of money consumers have
questions.explanation: Effective demand requires both willingness and ability to pay at a particular price.

questions.stem: The law of demand states that, other things being equal,
options: the higher the price, the higher the quantity demanded
price and quantity demanded are unrelated
the higher the price, the lower the quantity demanded
questions.explanation: Price and quantity demanded are inversely related.

questions.stem: A movement along a demand curve is caused by a change in
options: the price of the commodity itself
questions.explanation: Only a change in own price moves along the curve; other determinants shift the curve.

questions.stem: Which of the following will shift the demand curve for bread to the right?
options: A fall in the price of bread
A rise in the price of yam, a substitute
A rise in the price of margarine, a complement
A fall in consumers' income where bread is a normal good
questions.explanation: A dearer substitute makes consumers switch to bread, increasing demand at every price.

questions.stem: Demand for labour by a construction firm is an example of

questions.explanation: Composite demand arises when one commodity has several different uses.

questions.explanation: Substitutes compete for the consumer's spending.

options: a Giffen good with positive income elasticity
questions.explanation: Income elasticity = −10% ÷ 25% = -0.4; a negative value indicates an inferior good.

questions.explanation: Cross elasticity = 20% ÷ 25% = 0.8. A positive value means the goods are substitutes.

questions.explanation: A rise in the price of one reduces demand for the other, typical of goods used together.

questions.stem: Demand for a commodity tends to be price-inelastic when
options: it takes a large proportion of income
it is a necessity with few close substitutes
consumers have a long time to adjust
questions.explanation: Necessities without substitutes are bought almost regardless of price.

questions.stem: A trader reduced the price of a shirt from ₦1000 to ₦800 and her weekly sales rose from 50 to 70 shirts. What happened to her total revenue and what does it show about demand?
options: It fell by ₦6,000; demand is inelastic
It did not change; demand is unitary
It rose by ₦6,000; demand is inelastic
It rose by ₦6,000; demand is elastic
questions.explanation: Revenue moved from ₦50,000 to ₦56,000. Revenue rising when price falls indicates elastic demand.

questions.stem: If the demand for a commodity has unitary elasticity, a fall in its price will
options: leave total expenditure on it unchanged
questions.explanation: With unitary elasticity the percentage rise in quantity exactly offsets the price fall.

questions.stem: A government wishing to raise more revenue from an excise tax should tax goods whose demand is
questions.explanation: With inelastic demand, quantity falls little when the tax raises the price, so revenue holds up.

questions.stem: Goods that are bought in larger quantities when their prices rise because they confer status on the buyer are called
questions.explanation: Veblen goods are prestige goods whose demand may rise with price; Giffen goods are inferior staples.

questions.stem: A Giffen good is one for which
options: a rise in price leads to a rise in quantity demanded because it is a strongly inferior staple
price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions
questions.explanation: For a Giffen good the strong negative income effect outweighs the substitution effect.

questions.stem: The demand function for a product is Qd = 120 − 4P. How many units will be demanded at a price of ₦15?
An increase in demand, as distinct from an increase in quantity demanded, is shown by
options: a movement down the demand curve
a movement up the demand curve
a shift of the demand curve to the right
a shift of the demand curve to the left
questions.explanation: A change in demand (from non-price factors) shifts the whole curve.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a determinant of the demand for a commodity?
options: The cost of producing the commodity
questions.explanation: Production costs affect supply, not demand.

questions.stem: A perfectly elastic demand curve facing a firm means that
options: the firm can raise price without losing customers
the firm can sell any quantity at the ruling price but nothing above it
total revenue is constant at all prices
questions.explanation: A horizontal demand curve implies infinite elasticity at the market price.

questions.stem: Knowledge of price elasticity of demand helps a monopolist mainly to
options: determine the wages to pay workers
decide whether a price change will raise or lower total revenue
decide where to locate the factory
questions.explanation: Elasticity shows how revenue responds to price changes.

questions.stem: Utility in economics means
options: the usefulness of a good to society
the satisfaction derived from consuming a good or service
questions.explanation: Utility is the satisfaction a consumer obtains from consumption.

questions.stem: The law of diminishing marginal utility states that
options: total utility always falls as consumption rises
as more units of a good are consumed, the additional satisfaction from each extra unit eventually falls
questions.explanation: Each successive unit adds less satisfaction than the previous one.

questions.explanation: Negative extra satisfaction reduces the total.

questions.stem: A consumer spending her income on two goods X and Y is in equilibrium when
questions.explanation: Equal marginal utility per naira across goods maximises total satisfaction.

questions.stem: An indifference curve shows
options: combinations of two goods a consumer can afford
combinations of two goods that give a consumer the same level of satisfaction
the quantities of a good demanded at different prices
the output a firm can produce with given inputs
questions.explanation: Every point on an indifference curve yields equal utility.

questions.stem: The budget line of a consumer shows
options: combinations of goods yielding equal satisfaction
the change in utility as income rises
all combinations of two goods that can be bought with a given income at given prices
the prices of goods over time
questions.explanation: The budget line is the consumer's affordability constraint.

questions.stem: Using indifference curve analysis, the consumer is in equilibrium where
options: the budget line cuts the vertical axis
the budget line is tangent to the highest attainable indifference curve
the indifference curve is furthest from the origin
questions.explanation: At tangency the marginal rate of substitution equals the price ratio.

questions.stem: If a consumer's income rises while the prices of goods remain unchanged, the budget line will
options: shift outward parallel to the original line
shift inward parallel to the original line
questions.explanation: Higher income with constant relative prices moves the whole line out without changing its slope.

questions.stem: If the price of good X (on the horizontal axis) falls while income and the price of Y remain constant, the budget line will
options: pivot outward along the X-axis while its Y-intercept stays the same
questions.explanation: Only the maximum affordable quantity of X increases, so the line swings out along the X-axis.

questions.stem: Two indifference curves of the same consumer cannot intersect because
options: that would imply one combination gives two different levels of satisfaction
the budget line would become vertical
prices would have to be equal
the consumer would be irrational if he saved
questions.explanation: An intersection contradicts the assumption that higher curves represent higher satisfaction.

questions.stem: Ngozi was willing to pay ₦1,500 for a handbag but bought it for ₦1,100. Her consumer surplus is
questions.explanation: Consumer surplus = what she was willing to pay − what she paid = ₦400.

questions.stem: The concept of ordinal utility assumes that consumers
options: measure satisfaction in units called utils
have constant marginal utility of money
derive equal utility from all goods
can rank combinations of goods in order of preference without measuring satisfaction
questions.explanation: Ordinal utility only needs rankings; cardinal utility assumes measurable utils.

questions.stem: A student has ₦6,000 to spend on biscuits at ₦300 each and soft drinks at ₦200 each. The maximum number of soft drinks she can buy if she buys 8 biscuits is
questions.explanation: 8 biscuits cost ₦2,400; the remaining ₦3,600 buys 18 drinks at ₦200.

questions.stem: Supply refers to
options: the total stock of a commodity in existence
the quantity consumers want to buy
the quantity of a commodity producers are willing and able to offer for sale at a given price over a period
the quantity of goods in a warehouse
questions.explanation: Supply is the amount offered for sale at each price over a period.

questions.stem: The law of supply states that, other things being equal,
options: less is supplied at higher prices
more is supplied at higher prices than at lower prices
questions.explanation: Price and quantity supplied are positively related.

questions.stem: Which of the following will shift the supply curve of tomatoes to the left?
options: A fall in the price of tomatoes
A disease outbreak that destroys tomato farms
A subsidy given to tomato farmers
questions.explanation: Anything that reduces the ability to supply at every price shifts supply leftward.

questions.stem: Beef and hides are examples of goods in
questions.explanation: Producing beef automatically yields hides, so they are supplied jointly.

questions.stem: A farmer who can use his land to grow either maize or sorghum is faced with
questions.explanation: The products compete for the same resources: more of one means less of the other.

questions.stem: The supply of sugar from both sugar cane and sugar beet is an example of
questions.explanation: Composite supply arises when a commodity comes from several sources.

The supply of agricultural produce is usually inelastic in the short run because
options: farmers do not respond to prices
it takes time to grow more crops after prices rise
questions.explanation: Production lags (the gestation period) prevent quick output changes.

questions.stem: A vertical supply curve indicates that supply is
questions.explanation: Quantity supplied is fixed whatever the price.

questions.stem: A straight-line supply curve passing through the origin has elasticity of
questions.explanation: Any straight-line supply curve through the origin has unitary elasticity at all points.

questions.stem: An increase in the cost of fertiliser will
options: reduce the supply of maize, shifting the supply curve to the left
cause a movement up the maize supply curve
questions.explanation: Higher input costs reduce profitability at each price, so supply falls.

questions.stem: A change in quantity supplied, as opposed to a change in supply, is caused by
options: a change in the cost of inputs
a change in the price of the commodity itself
questions.explanation: Own price changes cause movements along the curve; other factors shift it.

questions.stem: Supply of a commodity is likely to be more elastic when
options: the good is perishable and cannot be stored
the production period is very long
producers hold large stocks and have spare capacity
factors of production are highly specialised
questions.explanation: Stocks and spare capacity allow quick increases in output when price rises.

questions.stem: The granting of a production subsidy to cement manufacturers will
options: shift the demand curve for cement to the left
shift the supply curve of cement to the right
shift the supply curve of cement to the left
leave the supply of cement unchanged
questions.explanation: A subsidy reduces production cost, so more is offered at each price.

options: a fall in the quantity supplied
questions.explanation: Above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.

questions.stem: Price control (maximum price legislation) commonly leads to
options: a rise in the official price
questions.explanation: Shortages created by a ceiling price encourage rationing, queues and illegal resale.

questions.stem: If demand increases while supply remains unchanged, equilibrium price and quantity will
questions.explanation: A rightward shift in demand along an upward-sloping supply curve raises both.

questions.stem: An increase in supply with demand unchanged will result in
options: a higher price and a higher quantity
a lower price and a lower quantity
a higher price and a lower quantity
a lower equilibrium price and a higher equilibrium quantity
questions.explanation: Supply shifting right moves down the demand curve.

questions.stem: If both demand and supply of a commodity increase by the same amount, then
options: equilibrium price rises while quantity remains unchanged
equilibrium price falls and quantity remains unchanged
equilibrium quantity rises while equilibrium price may remain unchanged
questions.explanation: Equal rightward shifts raise quantity; the price effects offset each other.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a function of the price system?
questions.explanation: Prices act as signals and rations that allocate resources.

questions.stem: Rationing of goods by the government becomes necessary when
options: a maximum price is fixed below the equilibrium price
a minimum price is fixed above equilibrium
questions.explanation: A ceiling price creates shortages that must be shared out by non-price means.

questions.stem: A market in economics refers to
options: any arrangement through which buyers and sellers are brought into contact to exchange goods
only a physical place where goods are sold
a shop owned by a government agency
a place where farm produce is stored
questions.explanation: A market need not be a place; it is any mechanism for buyer–seller contact.

questions.explanation: Consumers pay ₦30 more; the producer bears ₦50 − ₦30 = ₦20.

questions.stem: The burden of an indirect tax falls wholly on consumers when demand for the taxed good is
questions.explanation: If quantity demanded cannot fall, the price rises by the full tax.

questions.stem: Hoarding of a commodity by traders in anticipation of higher prices will, in the short run,
options: increase market supply and lower the price
reduce market supply and raise the price
questions.explanation: Withholding stock shifts supply left, raising price.

questions.stem: In a factor market, the equilibrium wage is determined where
options: the minimum wage is fixed by law
the demand for labour equals the supply of labour
the marginal product of labour is zero
the firm's total revenue is maximised
questions.explanation: As in product markets, the wage clears the market where demand meets supply.

questions.explanation: A cheaper complement raises demand for the related good, increasing both its price and quantity.

questions.stem: In economics, production is the
options: manufacture of goods in factories only
creation of goods and services to satisfy human wants
questions.explanation: Production includes all activities that create utility, including services.

questions.stem: Guaranteed minimum prices for farmers are intended to
options: protect farmers' incomes from sharp falls in market prices
lower the price of food to consumers
raise the price of imported fertiliser
questions.explanation: A price floor assures farmers of a minimum return.

questions.stem: An agricultural policy aimed at increasing food production through mass mobilisation and supply of inputs is an example of
questions.explanation: Several Nigerian programmes sought food self-sufficiency by mobilising farmers and providing inputs.

questions.stem: Mechanised agriculture involves
options: the use of only hoes and cutlasses
the use of machines such as tractors and harvesters
questions.explanation: Mechanisation replaces manual labour with machines.

questions.stem: Localisation of industry refers to
options: the choice of site by a single firm
the concentration of firms in a particular industry in one area
questions.explanation: Localisation is the clustering of an industry in a district.

questions.stem: An industry located close to its source of raw materials is likely to use raw materials that are
options: light and highly perishable finished goods
questions.explanation: Weight-losing materials are cheaper to process near their source, e.g. cement near limestone.

questions.stem: A bakery is usually located close to its market because
options: it needs large amounts of water
its product is perishable and needed fresh daily
questions.explanation: Perishable products are made near consumers.

questions.stem: Import substitution industrialisation means
options: setting up local industries to produce goods that were formerly imported
questions.explanation: It replaces imports with domestic production.

questions.stem: Export Processing Zones are established mainly to
options: process imported food for local use
attract investment in production for export by offering incentives
questions.explanation: EPZs offer tax and customs incentives to export-oriented firms.

questions.stem: A disadvantage of the localisation of industries is
options: regional unemployment when the main industry declines
questions.explanation: Dependence on one industry exposes the area to structural unemployment.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of industrialisation to a developing economy?
options: Diversification of the economy and creation of jobs
Reduction in the use of local raw materials
questions.explanation: Industry broadens the production base and provides employment.

questions.stem: Indigenisation policy was intended to
options: increase the participation of citizens in the ownership of businesses
reduce the number of local entrepreneurs
questions.explanation: Indigenisation reserved certain enterprises or equity shares for citizens.

questions.stem: A major problem limiting industrialisation in Nigeria is
options: erratic power supply that raises production costs
lack of demand for manufactured goods
questions.explanation: Firms rely on costly self-generation when public power is unreliable.

questions.stem: Which of the following determines the size of a firm?
options: The size of the market for its product
The age of the managing director
questions.explanation: Market size, capital availability and technology influence firm size.

questions.stem: Small-scale industries are important in developing countries because they
options: always enjoy large economies of scale
questions.explanation: They need little capital and absorb much labour.

questions.stem: The strategy of industrialisation that encourages domestic firms to produce for foreign markets is
questions.explanation: Export-led industrialisation targets foreign demand.

marketing petroleum products at filling stations
questions.explanation: Upstream covers finding and extracting crude oil.

questions.topic: Natural Resources and the Nigerian Economy

questions.topic: Natural Resources and the Nigerian Economy
questions.stem: Backward linkage in the oil industry occurs when the industry
options: stimulates local production of inputs it uses, such as pipes and services
questions.explanation: Backward linkages create demand for inputs; forward linkages supply outputs to other industries.

questions.topic: Natural Resources and the Nigerian Economy

questions.explanation: Using the oil industry's output as inputs for other industries is a forward linkage.

questions.topic: Natural Resources and the Nigerian Economy

questions.explanation: Revenue and foreign exchange swing with world oil prices.

questions.topic: Natural Resources and the Nigerian Economy
questions.stem: A major negative effect of oil exploration on host communities is
options: environmental pollution of land and water
questions.explanation: Spills and gas flaring damage farmland and fisheries.

questions.topic: Natural Resources and the Nigerian Economy
questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-oil natural resource found in Nigeria?
questions.explanation: Limestone is a solid mineral used for cement.

questions.topic: Natural Resources and the Nigerian Economy
questions.stem: The state-owned oil company in Nigeria participates in the oil industry mainly through
options: joint ventures with international oil companies
selling fuel only to neighbouring countries
questions.explanation: The national oil company holds equity in joint ventures and production-sharing contracts.

questions.topic: Natural Resources and the Nigerian Economy
questions.stem: The "Dutch disease" refers to
options: a rise in agricultural exports after devaluation
the decline of other export sectors following a natural-resource boom
questions.explanation: Resource booms raise the exchange rate and costs, hurting agriculture and manufacturing.

questions.topic: Natural Resources and the Nigerian Economy

questions.stem: A business owned and controlled by one person is a
questions.explanation: Sole proprietors own and manage alone.

questions.stem: A major disadvantage of a sole proprietorship is
questions.explanation: The owner's personal assets can be taken to pay business debts.

questions.stem: Limited liability means that shareholders
options: are not liable for any losses
can lose no more than the amount they invested in shares
must pay all company debts personally
questions.explanation: Shareholders' liability is limited to their share capital.

questions.stem: A sleeping partner is one who
options: manages the business but contributes no capital
contributes capital but takes no part in management
questions.explanation: Dormant partners invest but do not run the business.

questions.stem: Cooperative societies are run on the principle of
questions.explanation: Democratic control is a cooperative principle regardless of shareholding.

questions.stem: A public limited company differs from a private limited company in that it
options: can invite the general public to buy its shares
questions.explanation: Only a public company may offer shares to the public.

questions.stem: Public enterprises are established mainly to
options: provide essential services in the public interest
questions.explanation: Public corporations provide utilities and strategic services.

questions.stem: A major problem of public enterprises in many developing countries is
questions.explanation: Political appointments and interference weaken management.

questions.stem: Privatisation means
options: the transfer of ownership of public enterprises to private investors
making public enterprises charge market prices while remaining government-owned
questions.explanation: Ownership moves from the state to private hands.

questions.stem: Commercialisation of a public enterprise means
options: selling all its shares to the public
handing it over to a foreign company
running it on a profit-oriented basis while government retains ownership
questions.explanation: Commercialised enterprises must cover costs or make profits without subsidies.

questions.stem: Ploughing back profits as a source of finance means
options: retaining earnings in the business for expansion
questions.explanation: Retained profits are internal finance.

questions.stem: The highest decision-making body of a joint-stock company, at which shareholders vote, is the
questions.explanation: Shareholders exercise control through the general meeting.

questions.stem: Which of the following explains why many small firms survive alongside large firms?
options: They enjoy greater economies of scale
They have easier access to the stock exchange
The market for their product is small or highly personalised
They have limited liability in all cases
questions.explanation: Small markets, personal services and flexibility favour small firms.

questions.stem: In a partnership without a written agreement, profits are usually shared
questions.explanation: In the absence of agreement, the law presumes equal sharing.

questions.stem: Population census is
options: the registration of births and deaths
an official count of the people living in a country at a particular time
the movement of people from rural to urban areas
questions.explanation: A census enumerates the entire population at a point in time.

questions.stem: According to Thomas Malthus, population tends to increase
options: in arithmetic progression while food increases geometrically
in geometric progression while food supply increases in arithmetic progression
at the same rate as food supply
questions.explanation: Malthus argued population would outstrip food unless checked.

questions.stem: Optimum population is the population size at which
options: output per head is at its maximum
total output is at its maximum
there is no unemployment at all
questions.explanation: Optimum population maximises income per head given resources and technology.

questions.stem: A country is said to be over-populated when
options: its population is large in absolute terms
its death rate exceeds its birth rate
its population is greater than its resources can efficiently support
questions.explanation: Over-population is relative to resources, not just total numbers.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical town, there are 4,500 people aged 0–14, 5,000 aged 15–64 and 500 aged 65 and above. The dependency ratio is
questions.explanation: Dependency ratio = (dependants ÷ working-age) × 100 = 5,000 ÷ 5,000 × 100 = 100%.

questions.stem: If the crude birth rate of a country is 38 per 1,000 and the crude death rate is 12 per 1,000, the rate of natural increase is
questions.explanation: Natural increase = (38 − 12) per 1,000 = 26 per 1,000 = 2.6%.

questions.stem: A population with a high proportion of people under 15 years of age is described as
questions.explanation: Many children means a broad-based, young age structure.

questions.stem: A major problem associated with conducting a census in Nigeria is
options: inflation of figures for political and revenue-sharing advantage
questions.explanation: Population figures affect political representation and revenue allocation, encouraging inflated counts.

questions.stem: The occupational distribution of population refers to
options: how the working population is spread across different occupations or sectors
how people are spread across age groups
the ratio of males to females
the spread of people between towns and villages
questions.explanation: It shows employment by sector, e.g. primary, secondary, tertiary.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a likely consequence of a rapidly growing population in a poor country?
options: A fall in the dependency ratio
A rise in savings per head
Pressure on social amenities such as schools and hospitals
questions.explanation: Rapid growth strains infrastructure and services.

questions.stem: A population policy aimed at reducing the rate of population growth would most likely include
options: tax relief for every additional child
education on family planning and girl-child education
questions.explanation: Family planning and female education lower fertility rates.

questions.stem: Migration of people from villages to cities is known as
questions.explanation: Movement from rural to urban areas.

questions.stem: One importance of population census to economic planning is that it
options: provides data for planning social services and infrastructure
questions.explanation: Planners need population size and structure to provide schools, hospitals and housing.

questions.stem: The sex ratio of a population refers to
options: the proportion of the population that is working
the number of births per 1,000 people
the ratio of urban to rural dwellers
the number of males per 100 (or 1,000) females
questions.explanation: Sex ratio compares males to females.

questions.stem: International trade arises mainly because
options: all countries produce the same goods
countries differ in their resources and costs of production
questions.explanation: Differences in factor endowments create gains from specialisation and exchange.

questions.stem: The principle of comparative advantage states that a country should specialise in producing goods
options: which it produces in the largest quantities
in which it has an absolute advantage only
that it cannot produce at all
in which its opportunity cost is lowest
questions.explanation: Trade benefits both countries when each specialises where its relative cost is lower.

questions.stem: In country A one worker can produce 20 bags of rice or 10 rolls of cloth; in country B one worker can produce 12 bags of rice or 4 rolls of cloth. On the basis of comparative cost, A should specialise in
options: cloth, while B specialises in rice
rice, while B specialises in cloth
neither, because B has no absolute advantage
questions.explanation: Cost of 1 cloth: A gives up 2 rice, B gives up 3 rice, so A has comparative advantage in cloth; B's cost of rice (1/3 cloth) is lower than A's (1/2 cloth).

questions.stem: Using the same figures (A: 20 rice or 10 cloth per worker; B: 12 rice or 4 cloth per worker), the opportunity cost of one roll of cloth in country B is
questions.explanation: In B, 4 cloth cost 12 rice, so 1 cloth costs 12 ÷ 4 = 3 bags of rice.

questions.stem: The balance of trade is the difference between
options: the value of visible exports and visible imports
all receipts and payments of a country
questions.explanation: Balance of trade covers only goods (visibles).

questions.stem: A country recorded visible exports ₦7,200m, visible imports ₦5,900m, invisible exports ₦1,100m and invisible imports ₦2,600m. Its balance of trade is
questions.explanation: Balance of trade = 7,200 − 5,900 = +1,300m (surplus).

questions.stem: With visible exports ₦7,200m, visible imports ₦5,900m, invisible exports ₦1,100m and invisible imports ₦2,600m, the balance on current account is
Payment for shipping, insurance and tourism services between countries are recorded as
questions.explanation: Services are invisibles in the current account.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a measure for correcting a balance of payments deficit?
options: Restricting imports through tariffs and quotas
questions.explanation: Import restrictions reduce payments abroad.

questions.stem: Devaluation will improve a country's balance of payments only if
options: demand for its exports is perfectly inelastic
the demand for its exports and imports is sufficiently elastic
questions.explanation: Elastic demands ensure export earnings rise and import spending falls (the Marshall–Lerner condition).

questions.stem: If the index of export prices of a country is 132 and the index of import prices is 110, the terms of trade index is
questions.explanation: Terms of trade = (export price index ÷ import price index) × 100 = 120.

questions.stem: A country's terms of trade are said to improve when
options: its import prices rise relative to export prices
its export prices rise relative to its import prices
the volume of its exports falls
questions.explanation: Each unit of exports buys more imports.

questions.stem: An exchange rate is
options: the price of one currency expressed in terms of another
the rate of interest on foreign loans
the rate at which goods are exchanged in barter
questions.explanation: It is the rate at which currencies are exchanged.

questions.stem: Under a floating (flexible) exchange rate system, the exchange rate is determined by
options: the demand for and supply of the currency in the foreign exchange market
questions.explanation: Market forces set the rate.

questions.stem: If the exchange rate of a hypothetical currency moves from 800 units to 1,000 units per US dollar, the price in local currency of an imported machine costing $2,500 changes from
questions.explanation: Local price = $2,500 × rate; it rises by (1,000 − 800) ÷ 800 = 25% as the currency depreciates.

questions.stem: A quota as an instrument of trade restriction is
options: a limit on the quantity of a good that can be imported
questions.explanation: Quotas restrict import volumes.

questions.stem: Protectionism is often justified on the ground of
options: increasing the variety of imported goods
questions.explanation: Young industries may need temporary protection to grow.

questions.stem: The direction of a country's foreign trade refers to
options: the types of goods it trades
the countries with which it trades
questions.explanation: Direction is about trading partners; composition is about commodities.

questions.stem: Nigeria's exports are dominated by
questions.explanation: Oil and gas have long been Nigeria's main exports.

questions.stem: Dumping in international trade refers to
options: disposing of waste in the sea
selling goods abroad at prices below their cost or home-market price
questions.explanation: Dumping undercuts producers in the importing country.

questions.stem: ECOWAS was established mainly to
options: provide loans to all developing countries
promote economic integration among West African states
questions.explanation: ECOWAS aims at regional economic cooperation and integration.

questions.stem: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) mainly assists member countries by
options: providing short-term finance to correct balance of payments problems
fixing the price of crude oil
questions.explanation: The IMF supports BOP stability and the international monetary system.

questions.stem: The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) is part of the
questions.explanation: IBRD is the main lending arm of the World Bank Group.

questions.stem: The World Trade Organization (WTO) is mainly concerned with
options: promoting freer trade and settling trade disputes among members
providing loans for roads and dams
questions.explanation: WTO administers trade agreements and resolves disputes.

questions.stem: The United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) seeks mainly to
options: promote the trade and development interests of developing countries
questions.explanation: UNCTAD focuses on trade and development of poorer countries.

questions.stem: The African Development Bank (ADB) mainly
options: issues the currency of African countries
provides development finance for projects in African countries
questions.explanation: The ADB finances economic and social development in Africa.

questions.stem: The Economic Commission for Africa (ECA) is an agency of the
questions.explanation: The ECA is one of the UN regional commissions.

questions.stem: A customs union differs from a free trade area in that members of a customs union
options: adopt a common external tariff against non-members
questions.explanation: Both remove internal tariffs, but a customs union also harmonises external tariffs.

questions.stem: One benefit of ECOWAS to Nigeria is
options: an end to all imports from outside Africa
a wider market for Nigerian goods within the sub-region
fixed world prices for crude oil
questions.explanation: Regional integration enlarges markets for member producers.

questions.stem: The OECD is made up mainly of
questions.explanation: OECD members are largely high-income economies.

questions.stem: The African Union replaced the
questions.explanation: The AU succeeded the OAU.

questions.stem: The European Union is an example of
options: economic and political integration among countries in one region
questions.explanation: The EU integrates trade, policies and, for many members, currency.

questions.topic: Factors of Production and their Theories
questions.stem: Capital as a factor of production refers to
options: man-made goods used to produce other goods
questions.explanation: Machines, tools and buildings are capital goods.

questions.topic: Factors of Production and their Theories
questions.stem: A distinctive feature of land as a factor of production is that it
questions.explanation: The total quantity of land cannot be increased.

questions.topic: Factors of Production and their Theories
questions.stem: According to the marginal productivity theory, a firm will employ labour up to the point where
options: the wage equals the average product of labour
marginal product of labour is zero
the wage equals the marginal revenue product of labour
questions.explanation: Hiring stops where the extra revenue from a worker equals the wage.

questions.topic: Factors of Production and their Theories
questions.stem: Economic rent is
options: the rent paid on a house
any payment to a factor above its transfer earnings
the minimum payment to keep a factor in its present use
questions.explanation: Transfer earnings keep a factor in use; the surplus above it is economic rent.

questions.topic: Factors of Production and their Theories
questions.stem: An engineer earns ₦250,000 a month. The most she could earn in her next best job is ₦180,000. Her economic rent is
questions.explanation: Economic rent = earnings − transfer earnings = ₦70,000.

questions.topic: Factors of Production and their Theories
questions.stem: Unemployment that occurs when workers are between jobs is
questions.explanation: Frictional unemployment is temporary job-search unemployment.

questions.topic: Factors of Production and their Theories
questions.stem: Unemployment caused by a long-term decline in an industry or a change in technology is
questions.explanation: Mismatches between workers' skills and available jobs cause structural unemployment.

questions.topic: Factors of Production and their Theories
questions.stem: Unemployment resulting from a general fall in aggregate demand during a recession is
questions.explanation: It follows the trade cycle.

questions.topic: Factors of Production and their Theories
questions.stem: Disguised unemployment is common in peasant agriculture because
options: farmers are paid very high wages
more people work on a farm than are needed, so the marginal product of some is near zero
farm work is seasonal in nature
all farm labour is fully employed
questions.explanation: Removing some workers would not reduce output.

questions.topic: Factors of Production and their Theories
questions.stem: Mobility of labour refers to
options: the movement of workers by vehicles
the ease with which workers move between jobs or places
the supply of labour by households
questions.explanation: Occupational and geographical mobility.

questions.topic: Factors of Production and their Theories
questions.stem: Which of the following can reduce the occupational mobility of labour?
options: Low cost of housing in other areas
The need for long periods of specialised training
questions.explanation: Specialised skills make switching occupations difficult.

questions.topic: Factors of Production and their Theories
questions.stem: A hypothetical country has a labour force of 50 million, of whom 44 million are employed. The unemployment rate is
questions.explanation: Unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labour force × 100 = 6 ÷ 50 × 100 = 12%.
